Variants.Content: In 1259 devotion to the Eucharist is expressed through local feasts, sermons, processions and the choices of individual bishops. At Liège, the earlier visions and advocacy associated with Juliana of Cornillon have helped keep a special observance under discussion, but it is not yet a universal feast of the Latin Church. Reports about a bleeding host at Bolsena and the later papal action belong to future years, as does the familiar account of Thomas Aquinas composing a complete liturgy for a newly established feast. A priest may support a local celebration or question its expense; a town may organise a procession according to its own customs. The practice is real but uneven, and its eventual reach remains unknown.

In 1259 a cleric may know the feast promoted at Liege through Juliana of Mont Cornillon and local episcopal support. Its observance has not yet become a universal calendar rule. Teaching about the Eucharist, arranging a service and securing approval remain local concerns; later papal legislation and elaborate civic processions must not be projected onto every parish.

A villager hearing of a new Eucharistic observance asks when the parish will celebrate it and what work must stop. Candles, cloth and attendance cost households time and money, even when devotion is sincere. Customs differ between dioceses in 1259; a spectacular later procession cannot be assumed to pass every village church at the same appointed hour.
